You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

### arc_scale_and_mirror_a_quadrant_template_around_color_2_squares 
 For a grid divided by a color-1 cross, when the top-left quadrant contains a motif with a 2x2 color-2 core and the other quadrants contain square color-2 seeds, use the top-left motif as a template. Scale each motif component by target_side/2 around the core and orient it to the destination quadrant: horizontal reflection in the top-right, vertical reflection in the bottom-left, and 180-degree rotation in the bottom-right. Preserve the source quadrant and cross. Apply only when demonstrations support this structure. This rule was validated on two demos (target sides 1-4) and a correct test with target sides 1, 2, and 3.

### arc_quadrant_mask_expansion 
 For even-sized ARC grids that visibly divide into four equal quadrants, consider this rule only when the upper quadrants encode output dimensions and the lower quadrants form a source-and-mask pair. Count nonzero cells in the top-left quadrant for output height and in the top-right quadrant for output width. Use the bottom-left as the source and the bottom-right as a block mask: expand each source cell into a bottom-right-sized block, preserving nonzero mask colors and replacing mask zeros with that source cell's color, then crop to the counted output dimensions. If the bottom-right is entirely zero, the demonstrated variant is a direct crop of the bottom-left. Confirm the quadrant roles and output dimensions against examples before applying.

### arc_quadrant_stencil_fill_and_expand 
 For ARC inputs visibly divided into equal quadrants, consider whether the bottom-right quadrant is a repeating stencil whose zero cells are filled using the bottom-left quadrant. Confirm this structure against demonstrations before applying. In the demonstrated solid-data case, the bottom-left quadrant is a single solid color: tile the bottom-right pattern with its zero cells filled by that color, then crop to height equal to the count of nonzero cells in the top-left quadrant and width equal to the count of nonzero cells in the top-right quadrant. In the demonstrated varying-data case, bottom-left values supply fill colors for repeated bottom-right stencil tiles, producing an expanded output (the 8x8-to-16x16 example). A solved test had 16 ones in the top-left, 4 fives in the top-right, solid 9 in the bottom-left, and a 3/0 checkerboard stencil; its output was a 16x4 checkerboard of 3 and 9. One demo with an all-zero bottom-right produced the bottom-left pattern as output, but treat that only as an observed fallback, not a general rule.

### arc_four_quadrant_count_guided_tile_expansion 
 For even-sized ARC grids that visibly split into four equal quadrants, consider this rule only when the examples support it: the output height is the number of nonzero cells in the upper-left quadrant, and the output width is the number of nonzero cells in the upper-right quadrant. Tile the lower-right quadrant periodically to those dimensions. Preserve its nonzero cells; for each zero at output coordinate (r,c), fill it with the lower-left quadrant cell at (r // q, c // q), where q is the quadrant side length. Validate the quadrant structure, dimensions, and cell mapping against available examples before applying.
